hooks.text: Sunlight feels instant, but its energy spent 100,000 years escaping the core.
100,000 years is how long it takes sunlight to escape the Sun.
Why does sunlight take 100,000 years to reach the surface of our Sun?

title: The 100,000-Year Journey of a Single Sunbeam
description: Discover why sunlight is an ancient relic while ghost particles called neutrinos escape the Sun in seconds.

beats.text: Sunlight feels instant, but its energy spent 100,000 years escaping the core.
beats.visual: Solar internal structure diagram showing core and radiation zone

beats.text: Deep inside our star's core, nuclear fusion reactions convert four protons into helium, raw energy, and ghostlike neutrinos.
beats.visual: Diagram of the proton-proton nuclear fusion chain

beats.text: Light particles called photons begin an epic, 100,000-year obstacle course, constantly bouncing between dense solar particles.
beats.visual: Illustration of photon random walk in the solar radiation zone

beats.text: This slow process, called radiation diffusion, delays that energy for approximately 100,000 years before it finally reaches the surface.
beats.visual: Cross-section of the Sun showing core and surface layers

beats.text: However, nearly massless ghost particles called neutrinos interact so weakly that they fly straight through the Sun's layers.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of a neutrino passing through matter

beats.text: Detecting these ghost particles proves the Sun is still active deep within.
beats.visual: Photograph of the Borexino detector in the Gran Sasso laboratory

beats.text: Meaning the sunlight hitting your skin today is an ancient relic.
beats.visual: Close-up of human skin in bright sunlight
